extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour theory, rhetoric, philosophy, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Reading/analysis of classical and historical theories that explain laughter and ridicule—especially Aristotle, classical rhetoricians, Stoics/Christian critics, Hobbes—focusing on superiority and related social, moral, and rhetorical dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridiculousness (Aristotle/Sully formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridiculousness may be 'defined as a mistake or deformity which produces no pain or deformity to others' (Sully citing Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as evidence for classing Aristotle as a superiority theorist; emphasizes that comic figures are depicted as 'worse than the average' and that the ridiculed condition must not inflict real pain on others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of pain in comedy (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle contrasts comedy and tragedy by noting the absence of pain in comedy: the audience laughs rather than shares the characters' pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy permits contemplation of discrepant aspects of life 'in a painless manner'—theorists should distinguish audience's affective response (laughter vs pity) when classifying genres or interpreting comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from a feeling of superiority: we perceive another's deformity/misfortune/absurdity and feel superior, which produces laughter (as in Aristotle and Hobbes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a motivational/comparative account: laughter follows a cognitive comparison that produces 'sudden glory' or pleasurable superiority. Use this framework to interpret jokes that target infirmities, mistakes, or social inferiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical use of ridicule (Aristotle quoting Gorgias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule can be persuasively useful: 'we ought to worst our opponent’s earnest with mockery, and his mockery with earnest' (Gorgias, quoted approvingly by Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for persuaders: humour can undermine an overly earnest rival. But not all humour is suitable—speakers must select forms appropriate to their social standing and context (e.g., favor irony over buffoonery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability and taste in humour (Aristotle/Rhetoric & Nicomachean Ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms 'befit a free man and others do not' and one should 'take care to choose the appropriate sort of humour'; the 'middle disposition' shows wit, not buffoonery, and says things suitable to a virtuous man and gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider propriety, tact, and social norms: prefer innuendo to obscenity; avoid buffoonery if representing 'gentlemanly' wit. Tension exists between pragmatic persuasive aims and aesthetic/tastefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit and buffoonery
rubrics_metrics.description: Witty gentleman will respect propriety, show tact and prefer innuendo to obscenity; buffoonery is crude, linked with mockery and vulgarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying humour quality, identify whether the comic material relies on subtle irony/innuendo (valued) or on crude, humiliating, or boisterous buffoonery (criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/ethical limits on mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Since raillery can be a form of vilification and some forms of vilification are against the law, perhaps some forms of mockery should also be against the law (Aristotle's suggestion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ridicule, note potential legal/ethical boundaries and the risk that certain kinds of abusive mockery may be socially or legally impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class and hierarchy embedded in humour (Ancient to modern comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Ancient Athens, humour and irony were associated with the established, male order; superiority and 'gentlemanly' wit were classed, whereas buffoonery was expected from lower orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for social stratification: who is permitted to use what humour and who is the butt of jokes. Contemporary ideologies of equality complicate but do not erase these historical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as social reproduction of hierarchy (workplace example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour often flows downwards: superiors make jokes to inferiors; managers use irony and joking phrasing to issue commands and reproduce hierarchical relations (Holmes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate workplace humour by examining power dynamics: ironic utterance can function as an indirect order requiring both obedience and laughter, thereby reinforcing authority rather than dissolving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic vs aesthetic dilemma in rhetorical humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Orators face a choice between pragmatic effectiveness (using buffoonery to win arguments) and maintaining standards of taste and class (eschewing buffoonery in favor of tasteful irony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should weigh rhetorical efficacy against reputational/aesthetic costs; context and audience expectations determine which route is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic/Christian/Puritan critique of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions (Stoics, medieval theologians, Puritans) criticized frivolity and boisterous laughter; recommended limited, restrained laughter, acceptable when serving higher moral or disciplinary purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments influenced by moral/religious frameworks distinguish 'purposeless' laughter (condemned) from laughter in service of righteousness or discipline (permitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gendered norms around laughter (theological/historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theologians often distinguished between approved male laughter and disapproved female laughter (e.g., Abraham's joyous laughter vs Sarah's mocking laughter), attributing different social meanings to men's and women's laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider gendered expectations and how they shape whose laughter is legitimate or suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes's theory: laughter as 'sudden glory'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: 'the passion of laughter is nothing else but a sudden glory arising from sudden conception of some eminency in ourselves, by comparison with the infirmities of others, or with our own formerly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Hobbesian framework when interpreting laughter that seems rooted in comparative pleasure; note emphasis on novelty (the laughable must be new/unexpected) and focus on perceived inferiority/infirmity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes on target and novelty conditions for laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: people laugh at infirmities of others that set off their own abilities, and at jests whose wit 'consisteth in the elegant discovering' of another's absurdity; laughter ceases when things become 'stale or usual'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for what elicits laughter include comparative contrast (infirmity vs self) and novelty; analysts should check whether a comic event is both comparative and unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes on self-mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes concedes self-laughter but treats it as the same process: laughing at past infirmities because comparison shows present superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret self-directed humour as functioning through temporal comparison (past self inferior → present self superior), not as pure self-deprecation lacking superiority dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social dynamics critique of Hobbes (limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's model is individualist: communal laughter is explained as jealousy-driven conformity; it neglects spontaneity and the communicative/meaningful aspects of social laughter and underestimates forms of victimless humour (e.g., puns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criticisms to temper Hobbesian explanations: look for social, interactional, and non-comparative sources of humour when Hobbes's framework fails to account for observed cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical continuity of ridicule and elite condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: From ancient through medieval carnivals to modern times, masses mocked official texts and high culture; elites (philosophers, theologians) repeatedly condemned coarse laughter as offensive to morality or decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When situating contemporary humour historically, consider recurring patterns: carnivalized popular ridicule vs elite attempts to police laughter; this informs normative judgments about what is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative framing: permissible vs impermissible laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Across traditions there is an implicit evaluative frame: some laughter is permissible (restrained, purposeful, aligned with virtue), while purposeless, bawdy, or humiliating laughter is impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques and prescriptions should explicitly state the normative criteria (purpose, target, form, social standing) used to judge whether laughter is acceptable.
